sao-tiago.name: Santiago Square
sao-tiago.short: A medieval square of wooden balconies and café terraces, the heart of the UNESCO quarter
sao-tiago.long: Tradition says the apostle James brought an image of the Virgin here and placed it in a pagan temple, which gave the square its name. The Franks who came with Count Henry settled around it. Houses of the 17th and 18th centuries with timber galleries line the square, and the Gothic arcade of the old town hall leads through to the neighbouring Largo da Oliveira. Today it is the liveliest square in the old town: cafés, terraces and the Nicolinas festivities.
sao-tiago.history:
Legend takes the square back to the first Christian centuries: Saint James, São Tiago in Portuguese, brought an image of the Virgin here and set it in a pagan temple. Documents mention the square over many centuries, and it keeps its medieval layout. The Franks who came to Portugal with Count Henry of Burgundy settled nearby.

A porched chapel of Saint James stood in the square, an early 17th-century building on the site of an older, decayed chapel. It was a stage on the way to Santiago de Compostela. In July 1882 the town council decided to buy and demolish it to enlarge the square under a plan drawn up in the 1860s by the engineer Almeida Ribeiro. A law of May 1886 allowed the demolition, and in January 1887 the chapel came down despite protests. Today the outline of its plan is marked in the paving.

The houses with wooden balconies that look so romantic today were once thought slums. The square seldom appeared on old postcards: it was considered “unworthy”. In 1904 the council approved an extension of the square that meant pulling down three houses, and in 1911 a reader of the republican newspaper called for the whole quarter to be razed. Instead, in the last quarter of the 20th century the architect Fernando Távora renewed the square with a light hand and gave the chapel back to it symbolically, as a line on the ground.

One side of the square is closed by the old town hall, whose ground floor is a Gothic arcade: through it you pass into Largo da Oliveira. The square lies within the Historic Centre of Guimarães, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001. Every year during the students’ Nicolinas festivities it hosts the Maçãzinhas, the rite of the little apples that draws the whole town into the square.
facts: Legend says the apostle James named the square by bringing an image of the Virgin here.
The chapel of Saint James was demolished in January 1887; its plan is marked in the paving.
The arcade of the old town hall links the square to Largo da Oliveira.
Fernando Távora directed the square’s renewal in the late 20th century.
Part of the Historic Centre of Guimarães, a UNESCO site since 2001.
sao-tiago.tip: Evening is the best time, when café terraces fill the whole square. Look for the line in the paving that traces the plan of the demolished chapel. Go through the arcade of the old town hall into Largo da Oliveira, or up Rua de Santa Maria to the Dukes’ Palace and the castle.
